title: Disks and file systems: FAT against UFS2
subtitle: MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1, from raw sectors to files

slides.title: From a name to a sector
slides.caption: Drive letter, CDS and DPB on MS-DOS; GEOM providers on FreeBSD
slides.notes: Start from what a program names. On MS-DOS a drive letter selects a CDS entry, which points to the DPB built from the BPB at boot, which points to the driver unit; the driver turns a logical sector into CHS for INT 13h. On FreeBSD a path leads to a mounted file system, which is a consumer of a GEOM provider such as ada0p4; the PART class adds the partition offset and passes a bio to the disk.

slides.title: The Drive Parameter Block
slides.code:
dpb_drive           DB      ?           ; Logical drive # assoc with DPB (A=0,B=1,...)
dpb_UNIT            DB      ?           ; Driver unit number of DPB
dpb_sector_size     DW      ?           ; Size of physical sector in bytes
dpb_cluster_mask    DB      ?           ; Sectors/cluster - 1
dpb_cluster_shift   DB      ?           ; Log2 of sectors/cluster
dpb_first_FAT       DW      ?           ; Starting record of FATs
dpb_FAT_count       DB      ?           ; Number of FATs for this drive
dpb_root_entries    DW      ?           ; Number of directory entries
dpb_first_sector    DW      ?           ; First sector of first cluster
dpb_max_cluster     DW      ?           ; Number of clusters on drive + 1
⋮
dpb_first_access    DB      ?           ; This is initialized to -1 to force a media
                                        ; check the first time this DPB is used
dpb_next_dpb        DD      ?           ; Pointer to next Drive parameter block
dpb_next_free       DW      ?           ; Cluster # of last allocated cluster
dpb_free_cnt        DW      ?           ; Count of free clusters, -1 if unknown
slides.notes: One DPB per drive letter. Point at dpb_cluster_mask and dpb_cluster_shift: the kernel turns cluster numbers into sectors with shifts. dpb_next_free and dpb_free_cnt come back in Lab 7.3 and Exercise 7.5, where DPBINFO.C prints them.

slides.title: Partitions and disks in the official FreeBSD VM image
slides.notes: Real output of vhdpart.py on FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.vhd.xz. A GPT disk with a protective MBR of type EEh. Note that the EFI system partition is FAT: firmware everywhere reads FAT, which is part of the essay question.

slides.title: Two layouts
slides.caption: FAT keeps all metadata at the front; UFS2 repeats it in every cylinder group
slides.notes: Numbers are real: the lab floppy (sectors) and the root file system of the VM image (4 KB fragments). FAT: boot sector, two FATs side by side, fixed root directory, data. UFS2: superblock at 64 KB, then nine cylinder groups each with a superblock copy, bitmaps, 80,256 inodes and data.

slides.title: A directory entry is the file's whole description
slides.code:
dir_entry   STRUC
dir_name    DB      11 DUP (?)          ; file name
dir_attr    DB      ?                   ; attribute bits
dir_codepg  dw      ?                   ; code page DOS 4.00
dir_extcluster dw   ?                   ; extended attribute starting cluster
dir_attr2   db      ?                   ; reserved
dir_pad     DB      5  DUP (?)          ; reserved for expansion
dir_time    DW      ?                   ; time of last write
dir_date    DW      ?                   ; date of last write
dir_first   DW      ?                   ; first allocation unit of file
dir_size_l  DW      ?                   ; low 16 bits of file size
dir_size_h  DW      ?                   ; high 16 bits of file size
dir_entry   ENDS
callouts: Attributes: R H S V D A
Time and date packed in 16 bits each
First cluster; the FAT has the rest
slides.notes: Decode Output 7.4 live: 4916h is 9:08:44, 5D69h is 2026-11-09. Ask why a directory's size field is 0, and why two names for one file are impossible when the metadata lives here.

slides.title: ALLOCATE: next fit from dpb_next_free
slides.code:
mov     bx,es:[bp.dpb_next_free]
        cmp     bx,2
        ja      findfre
⋮
FINDFRE:
        INC     BX
⋮
aupk:
        invoke  UNPACK          ; check out this cluster
        jc      ads4            ; FAT error             [INTERR?]
        jnz     findfre         ; not free, keep on truckin

;   Have found a free cluster.  Chain it to the file
;
;       (BX) = found free cluster #
;       (DX) = current last cluster in file

        mov     es:[bp.dpb_next_free],bx        ; next time start search here
callouts: Start at the cursor, not at cluster 2
slides.notes: The search continues from the last cluster allocated. Apart from the wrap-around to cluster 2 at the end of the disk, the cursor is reset only when the DPB is rebuilt, which happens whenever the floppy driver answers 'don't know' to a media check, for example after an access to another drive. That is the whole explanation of Lab 7.3.

slides.title: Limits of the 4.00 formats

stats.label: cluster numbers of FAT16 (2 to FFF6h)
the old limit of the 16-bit sector count

slides.notes: DOS 4.00 added the 32-bit total in the extended BPB and 32-bit sector numbers in the kernel (HIGH_SECTOR). The IO.SYS table goes to 128 sectors per cluster, but 64 KB clusters overflow 16-bit byte counts in the utilities, so 2 GB is the practical limit. Exercise 7.2 asks for the derivation.

slides.title: The superblock of the official VM image (real)
slides.notes: From ufsx.py sb on the root partition copied out of the .vhd.xz with vhdpart.py. Every value is a field of struct fs in fs.h. fs_maxfilesize is computed by mkfs from bsize and NINDIR: 12 direct blocks plus single, double and triple indirect.

slides.title: struct ufs2_dinode: 256 bytes per file
slides.code:
struct ufs2_dinode {
        uint16_t        di_mode;        /*   0: IFMT, permissions; see below. */
        uint16_t        di_nlink;       /*   2: File link count. */
        uint32_t        di_uid;         /*   4: File owner. */
        uint32_t        di_gid;         /*   8: File group. */
        uint32_t        di_blksize;     /*  12: Inode blocksize. */
        uint64_t        di_size;        /*  16: File byte count. */
        uint64_t        di_blocks;      /*  24: Blocks actually held. */
        ufs_time_t      di_atime;       /*  32: Last access time. */
        ufs_time_t      di_mtime;       /*  40: Last modified time. */
        ufs_time_t      di_ctime;       /*  48: Last inode change time. */
⋮
                        ufs2_daddr_t    di_db /* 112: Direct disk blocks. */
                            [UFS_NDADDR];
                        ufs2_daddr_t    di_ib /* 208: Indirect disk blocks. */
                            [UFS_NIADDR];
slides.notes: Compare with the 32-byte DOS entry. Everything except the name is here; the directory only maps names to inode numbers. Pointers count 4 KB fragments: di_db[0] = 5057 for the root directory means byte 5057 x 4096 of the partition.

slides.title: Where is block n?
slides.caption: A FAT chain of links against direct and indirect pointers
slides.notes: Real data: A.DAT of Lab 7.3 and /boot/kernel/kernel of the VM image, 897 blocks, 12 direct and 885 through one indirect block at fragment 29112, placed right after the last direct block as ffs_blkpref_ufs2 says. Study case 7.A: byte 100,000 costs 195 links on the floppy, one array lookup on UFS2.

slides.title: Directory entries
slides.caption: FAT's entry is the metadata; UFS2's entry only names an inode
slides.notes: UFS directory records have variable length (d_reclen) inside 512-byte chunks; the last record of a chunk absorbs the free space. The root directory of the image is 20 records in 512 bytes, the last one 240 bytes long. Hard links are just two records with the same d_ino.

slides.title: Soft updates: roll back, write, roll forward
slides.code:
/*
 * Allocation dependencies are handled with undo/redo on the in-memory
 * copy of the data. A particular data dependency is eliminated when
 * it is ALLCOMPLETE: that is ATTACHED, DEPCOMPLETE, and COMPLETE.
 *
 * The ATTACHED flag means that the data is not currently being written
 * to disk.
 *
 * The UNDONE flag means that the data has been rolled back to a safe
 * state for writing to the disk. When the I/O completes, the data is
 * restored to its current form and the state reverts to ATTACHED.
 * The data must be locked throughout the rollback, I/O, and roll
 * forward so that the rolled back information is never visible to
callouts: Unsafe changes rolled back in the copy written
slides.notes: The goal: whatever subset of writes reaches the disk, the only damage is leaked blocks and inodes. SU+J adds a small journal so fsck_ffs replays instead of scanning. newfs -j runs tunefs -j enable after mkfs.

slides.title: Comparing the two, and the I/O path
FAT against UFS2
rows: Leaks only; background fsck or journal
slides.notes: Each row has a permalink in section 7.4. Be fair to FAT: it is tiny, needs no notion of users, and every firmware can read it. That is why the EFI partition of the FreeBSD image is FAT.

slides.title: The disk I/O path
slides.caption: INT 25h/26h bypass the DOS buffers; GEOM refuses writes under a mounted file system
slides.notes: DOS: BUFFERS=20 one-sector buffers, then the IO.SYS driver and INT 13h. INT 26h goes straight to the driver and does not update a buffer holding the same sector. FreeBSD: buffer and page cache, then GEOM; a write open of a provider that a mounted file system holds exclusively fails with EPERM.

slides.title: GEOM says no
slides.notes: UFS opens its provider with read, write and exclusive access (g_vfs_open). dd of=/dev/md0 then asks for write access and gets EPERM. kern.geom.debugflags=0x10 lifts the check on disks; its name says what the developers think of it.

slides.title: Labs 7.3 and 7.4: fragmentation and damage
bullets: 7.3: one batch file, two layouts (next-fit cursor)
7.4: setfat makes a lost chain and a cross-link
CHKDSK hangs: label + cross-link + media F0h
The kernel's IsEof accepts FF0h; CROSSLOOK does not
FILE0000.CHK dated 1994: SHL AL,CL loses the year
slides.notes: Two real bugs in the 1988 CHKDSK, both explained from the source: the second pass follows the label's cluster 0 into FAT entry 0 = FF0h and walks off the FAT; Systime shifts the year inside the 8-bit AL, so only 1980-1995 work.

slides.title: CROSSLOOK stops only at EOFVAL
slides.code:
CHLP:
        PUSH    BX                                         ;an014;bgb
        CALL    UNPACK                                     ;an014;bgb
        POP     BX                                         ;an014;bgb
        XCHG    SI,DI                                      ;an014;bgb
        CMP     SI,[EOFVAL]                                ;an014;bgb
        jae     chaindone                                  ;an014;bgb                      ;an014;bgb
;;;;;;;;JAE     Check_XA_Cross                             ;an014;bgb                      ;an014;bgb
        CALL    CROSSCHK                                   ;an014;bgb
        JZ      CHLP                                       ;an014;bgb
        JMP SHORT CROSSLINK                                ;an014;bgb
callouts: UNPACK(0) returns FAT[0] = FF0h on a 1.44 MB disk
FF0h < FF8h: treated as a cluster
The loop reads past the FAT table
slides.notes: Remove the volume label with DEBUG W (or empty files) and CHKDSK completes and reports the cross-link. On a hard disk, media F8h, FAT[0] is FF8h and the loop ends at once. The kernel fixed the same problem in IsEof in 1986.

In 7.7, IO.SYS is inode 304: root directory sector 19 times 16 entries per sector, entry 0.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: FAT: one global table, metadata in the directory entry
UFS2: inodes, bitmaps and data spread over cylinder groups
Finding byte n: n/cluster links against at most 3 indirect blocks
FAT repairs after the fact; soft updates order the writes
Raw disk writes: unchecked on DOS, refused by GEOM when mounted
slides.notes: Close with the essay question: FAT lost on every technical axis except simplicity and universality, and those turned out to matter most for removable media and firmware. Next module: memory.
